unit.title: Faith and Empire in the Medieval World

contentBlocks.text: A spiritual teaching can inspire people, but it takes a real institution to make that teaching an unavoidable, daily practice. Today, a world-history lens on Langar.

From a world-history perspective, one reason a new religious movement succeeds and lasts is whether it builds real institutions that put its core ideas into daily, physical practice — not just words. Langar, the free community kitchen, did exactly this for early Sikhi: it turned the abstract idea of equality (that all people, regardless of caste or status, deserve equal dignity) into a concrete, repeatable, unavoidable daily act — everyone sitting together, eating the same food. This is a genuine institution-building strategy historians recognize across many movements throughout world history: turning belief into shared, structured practice. Think about why a daily, physical practice might spread and sustain a belief more effectively than words alone.

You just analyzed Langar through a world-history lens: as an institution that made a belief into daily practice. Tomorrow we'll look at how a written scripture served a similar institution-building role.

objectives: Explain how Langar turned an abstract belief (equality) into a concrete daily institution
Apply a general world-history principle (institutions help movements endure) to a specific example
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's geographic/cultural context.
2. Introduce the institution-building analytical lens using Langar as the example.
3. Discuss why daily physical practice might sustain a belief more than words alone.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: the scripture as an institution.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on the concrete fact (Langar = everyone eating together = equality made real) before the more abstract 'institution-building' framing
Ready for more: ask them to think of a modern example of a daily practice that reinforces a belief or value
This connects directly to Langar content already covered in earlier Sikhi grades, but analyzes it from a genuinely different (world-history/institutional) angle rather than repeating the same content
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Langar turned the idea of equality into a concrete, repeatable daily act. 2. Everyone sitting together and eating the same food made equality unavoidable, not just an idea. 3. A daily, physical practice can sustain a belief more effectively than words alone because it's repeated and shared by everyone.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Addresses the C3 Framework History dimension's analytical skill of examining HOW religious/social movements build lasting institutions, applying a genuine world-history lens to content already introduced at a simpler level in earlier Sikhi grades.

generationData.instructions: Answer each question about Langar as an institution.

How did Langar make that belief unavoidable rather than optional?
